meta.title: Mentoring — Javier Aguilar
meta.description: Your business team is already building with agents. A one-day diagnosis of what they need to know so it holds up in production.

hero.title: Your business team is already building with agents
hero.subtitle: They are wiring tools to your real data without knowing which questions to ask. In one day I teach them the questions that matter — using the project they are actually building.

problem.title: It isn't that they can't code
body: People in product, operations, marketing and finance are building their own tools now. They describe what they want, an agent builds it, and it works. That part is real.

The problem isn't code quality — the agent writes decent code. It's that nobody ever told them which categories of risk exist: that having a login is not the same as being protected, that a key stays in the project's history after you delete it from the code, that by default nothing caps the bill.
You cannot ask about a space you don't know is there. An agent answers any question well — what it won't do is tell you which question you should have asked.
problem.closing: Your engineers can't review everything the rest of the company builds. Usually they're just the ones who inherit it.

situations.title: Two situations, one answer

cases.name: They are already building
cases.body: Nobody approved it — it just happened, because the tools got good. The risk is already there whether or not anyone is tracking it, and the people carrying it don't know which questions to ask.

cases.name: You would rather they didn't. Yet.
cases.body: Then the choice isn't between letting them build and stopping them. Teams pick these tools up with or without permission. The real choice is whether it happens deliberately, with the guardrails explained up front, or quietly. Teaching first costs a fraction of correcting later.

situations.closing: Either way what the team needs is the same — and it isn't a programming course. It's knowing which questions to ask, so you can hand them the tools without handing them the risk.

system.title: A system, not a course
system.subtitle: The whole thing is published. Read it and judge it before you talk to me.
system.loopBody: Specify, build, check, correct. Two of those four phases hand over to the agent completely — and they are exactly the two people mean when they say "programming". What is left is saying what you want and knowing whether you got it.
system.mapBody: Twelve categories where things go wrong, plus one of taste. For each one, three levels: knowing it exists, being able to ask about it, and having a view of your own. Nobody sits on the same level across the board — the profile comes out jagged, and that is exactly what the diagnosis measures.
system.assessmentCta: Where do you stand? Take the 13-question check →

Not building the product for you. That is consulting, and it is another door on the same site.
Not training in one specific tool. That is in its documentation, for free.

cta.title: Find out where the gaps are
cta.subtitle: A short call is enough to tell whether this helps you or not. If it does not, I will say so.

meta.title: Where are your gaps? — Javier Aguilar
meta.description: Thirteen questions about building software with agents. Find out which categories you didn't know were categories.

intro.title: Where are your gaps?
intro.subtitle: Thirteen questions, about two minutes. There is no score to beat — the useful result is finding a box you didn't know existed.
intro.note: Nothing is sent anywhere. The result stays in your browser unless you choose to share it at the end.

questions.prompt: You're starting something new. How do you put it to the agent?

options.text: I ask for small pieces one at a time and see where it gets me
I describe the features I want built
I say what the thing is for, and let it propose how before it writes anything
I match the tool and model to the job before I start

questions.prompt: You delete some test records while trying things out. Can that touch real users' data?

options.text: No — test and real are separate by definition
I don't know
Yes, if both are pointing at the same database
Yes — and that's why I check which environment I'm in before touching anything

questions.prompt: You delete the project and have the agent rebuild it from your description. What comes back?

options.text: Everything, if the description was good enough
I don't know
The code, but not what users had entered
The code — and the data only if there was a backup somewhere else

questions.prompt: It worked on Monday. It's Thursday and it doesn't. What decides whether you can get Monday back?

options.text: Whether the agent remembers what it changed
I don't know
Whether the changes were being saved as you went
That — and I ask for a save point before anything big, so Monday still exists

questions.prompt: You delete an API key from the code and save the change. Is it still exposed?

options.text: No, it's gone now
I don't know
Yes — it stays in the project's history
Yes, so deleting isn't enough: the key has to be replaced

questions.prompt: Your app has a login screen. Can anyone read the data without going through it?

options.text: No, that's what the login is for
I don't know
Yes, if the part that serves the data doesn't check who's asking
Yes — and it's worth checking one logged-in user can't read another's either

questions.prompt: You collect users' emails to send them updates. What does that require beyond a working form?

options.text: Nothing else — they typed it in themselves
I don't know
Their agreement to be contacted, and a way to delete them
That, plus not collecting what you don't need in the first place

questions.prompt: Nobody uses your app for a whole month. What does it cost you?

options.text: Nothing, since nobody used it
I don't know
Whatever's charged regardless of use — the database, the hosting
That — and a busy month has no ceiling unless you set one

questions.prompt: How many of the moving parts your app needs are run by someone else?

options.text: I couldn't name them
I don't know
I know roughly which ones aren't mine
I know, and I know what breaks first if one disappears

questions.prompt: It responds instantly for you. What does that tell you about three hundred people at once?

options.text: That it's fast, so it should cope
I don't know
Almost nothing — one user isn't a test of anything
Nothing, and what gives way first is worth asking about before it does

questions.prompt: The tests pass. What does that actually guarantee?

options.text: That the app works
I don't know
That the parts someone wrote a test for still behave
That — which is why what scares you is what needs a test

questions.prompt: You come back to the project after six months away. What does the agent find?

options.text: Whatever it finds — I hadn't thought about it
I don't know
Notes I keep up to date so it doesn't have to guess
Instructions written for it specifically, separate from what people read

questions.prompt: The agent hands you an interface. What happens next?

options.text: I keep it — it looks fine
Something feels off, but I couldn't say what
I can name what bothers me well enough to get it changed
I had a look in mind before it built anything

result.title: Your map
result.unknownLabel: boxes you didn't know were boxes

verdicts.many: Most of the risk you're carrying isn't in the categories you scored low on — it's in the ones you didn't know existed. That's the good news: they're the cheapest to fix, because knowing a category exists is enough to start asking.
verdicts.some: You've got the shape of it. The gaps left are the ones worth closing first, because you can't ask about what you don't know is there.
verdicts.few: You know the map. From here it's about depth in the categories where your project is actually betting something — not breadth.
verdicts.none: You know all thirteen exist. The question stops being what you know and becomes whether every box has someone checking it — you, a test, a service, or another person.

result.shareBody: I'll email you the map along with what to do about it. Reply to it and we can go through your project together.
result.mentoringLink: Or see how I do this with teams
result.subscribe: Also send me what I write about this
result.error: That didn't go through. Try again, or write to me directly.

why.Other people's data: it's the only one where the cost of getting it wrong isn't yours to pay
why.Who can get in: an open door gives no signal — it works exactly as well until someone finds it
why.Secrets: a leaked key is still there after you delete it, and nothing tells you
why.Code versus data: it's the one thing that can't be generated again
why.Getting back: it's the most common disaster in this field and the easiest one to avoid
why.What it costs: nothing caps it by default, and the bill arrives once the money is spent
why.Where your app lives: almost nobody deletes production on purpose — they delete it believing it was the test copy
why.Tests and breakage: without them every check is you guessing what happened in the middle
why.Holding load: nothing during building warns you, because while you build there's one user
why.Who you depend on: what fails isn't your code, it's something that stops existing
why.Six months on: mess doesn't slow you down, it slows down the agent you're relying on
why.What can be asked for: it caps everything else — you can't ask for what you don't know exists
why.Taste: nobody will ever tell you it's wrong, because it isn't — it's fine, and anonymous

result.harmPattern: More than one of your gaps is in the group where the damage lands on someone else. Those are worth closing before anything that only costs you money.
result.spreadPattern: Note the spread: you're at the top of the scale in some categories and at the bottom in others. That's normal — it's a map with holes, not a ladder — but the holes are where the surprises come from.
result.unknownLabelOne: box you didn't know was a box

devopsAgent.problem: Development teams spend countless hours on repetitive issue triage and resolution. Context switching between repositories and manual task coordination creates bottlenecks that slow down shipping.
devopsAgent.solution: A multi-agent system that automatically triages issues, researches context across repositories, and orchestrates parallel task execution. Agents collaborate to resolve issues while keeping humans informed at key decision points.
outcomes: ~50% reduction in issue triage time
Parallel execution across multiple repositories with session resume
Auto-fix CI failures and PR feedback iteration

complianceClassifier.problem: Classifying a business into the right industry code takes 10–30 minutes of manual research per entity — searching government registries, cross-referencing web presence, and interpreting ambiguous business activities. At scale, this becomes a bottleneck for merchant onboarding and KYB compliance workflows. Different jurisdictions use different classification systems (ANZSIC, SIC, NACE), and each client may enforce its own risk policy with distinct prohibited categories and thresholds.
complianceClassifier.solution: An AI-powered classification service that combines three intelligence sources: official government registries (ABR, NZBN, AUSTRAC), live web search for business activity research, and LLM reasoning for code assignment. Input data is first enriched from registries, then the AI analyzes web presence to determine business activities and map them to industry codes — validated against the official taxonomy hierarchy. A 4-tier risk engine evaluates the result: blacklist screening, code-to-risk mapping, keyword scanning with LLM disambiguation, and full LLM risk reasoning for ambiguous cases. Both the classification system and the risk policy are configurable per client.
outcomes: Classification accuracy above 90% with official registry cross-validation
Processing time under 1 minute per entity (vs. 10–30 minutes manual)
Configurable risk policies and classification systems per client
4-tier risk engine with hard-floor codes that cannot be overridden
Deployed in production for enterprise financial services clients

dataSourceAutomator.problem: Data engineering teams waste weeks researching data sources, writing specifications, building extraction pipelines, and deploying them. Each service needs a schema contract with the frontend, infrastructure provisioning, and end-to-end verification — a manual process that doesn't scale beyond a handful of services.
dataSourceAutomator.solution: A multi-agent pipeline that automates the entire lifecycle: research agents explore extraction methods, spec agents generate data models, coding agents build microservices with JSON schema contracts (search, detail, report, settings, config) that bridge backend and frontend, deployment agents push to Kubernetes via ArgoCD, and verification agents run automated checks across infrastructure, data contracts, and API responses. When tests fail, a code-fixer agent patches the code and redeploys automatically — with a LoopGuard that escalates to humans after 3 failed attempts on the same bug.
outcomes: 50+ microservices deployed through the pipeline
Automated deploy → verify → fix → redeploy feedback loop
JSON schema contract system bridging backend APIs and low-code frontend
Self-healing with LoopGuard: max 3 iterations per bug, then HITL escalation

mcpBitbucket.solution: A Model Context Protocol server that exposes Bitbucket's full API to LLMs. Manage repositories, create and review pull requests, trigger pipelines, and monitor builds—all through natural language.

TypeScript + Python implementations published on npm/PyPI
Open source with active maintenance

Published on npm and PyPI

mcpLangfuse.solution: A comprehensive MCP server for Langfuse observability. Access traces, manage datasets, query scores, and handle prompt versioning—all through your LLM interface.

Works with Langfuse Cloud and self-hosted

mcpAzure.solution: An MCP server that wraps Azure CLI operations — App Services, Storage accounts, Container Registry, and Application Insights — exposing them as tools that any LLM can call directly. Read-only by default.

Read-only operations for safe exploration
Covers App Services, Storage, ACR, and Application Insights

mcpKubernetes.problem: Debugging Kubernetes issues means running kubectl commands across multiple clusters, remembering namespace conventions, and parsing verbose JSON output. It's a constant context-switch away from the actual problem-solving.
mcpKubernetes.solution: An MCP server that wraps kubectl operations — pods, deployments, services, logs, and cluster diagnostics — making them accessible to LLMs as callable tools. Supports multi-cluster environments with configurable contexts.
outcomes: Query Kubernetes clusters through natural language
Multi-cluster support with context switching
Pod status, logs, deployments, and service diagnostics

steelPricing.problem: Steel buyers manage pricing across multiple suppliers, each with hundreds of tariff tables that change frequently. Calculating prices requires cross-referencing material specs, supplier agreements, and current rates — a manual process prone to errors and delays.
steelPricing.solution: A full pricing management platform with three AI integration points: a conversational assistant that fills calculation forms from natural language and queries pricing data, an email parser that interprets supplier price change notifications and suggests table updates (with human approval), and OCR-based PDF digitization that extracts tariff data from supplier documents for import.
outcomes: 925+ active pricing tables across 7 major steel suppliers
Three distinct AI integrations: assistant, email parsing, PDF digitization
Role-based access for purchasing, management, verification, and plant teams
All AI-suggested changes require human approval before applying

purchasingPlatform.problem: Managing Bills of Materials for steel infrastructure projects involves tracking thousands of line items across multiple suppliers, revisions, and procurement stages. Coordinating emails, categorizing materials, and summarizing plans is time-intensive manual work.
purchasingPlatform.solution: A purchasing management platform built for a steel corporation's Asia operations. AI is woven throughout: an assistant that answers questions about plans and data, automatic plan summarization, email generation for supplier communications, and intelligent material categorization when items aren't in the master database.
outcomes: 2,800+ BOM items processed across 11 active projects
AI-powered material categorization for unknown items
Automated plan summaries and supplier email generation
Trilingual support (English, Spanish, Chinese)

complianceAssistant.problem: Financial crime analysts spend hours manually reviewing verification reports, cross-referencing sanctions lists, PEP databases, and ownership structures across multiple screens. The review process is slow, error-prone, and doesn't scale.
complianceAssistant.solution: An AI assistant embedded directly in the compliance platform via iframe. Analysts query cases in natural language, get structured summaries of risk findings, UBO hierarchies, and screening results. The assistant can create and modify cases — but only after explicit human confirmation. PII is automatically redacted before storage, and all interactions are audit-logged.
outcomes: Structured LLM output via Zod schemas — summaries, tables, action cards, not free text
Human-in-the-loop for all write operations — the AI proposes, the analyst confirms
Semantic case search with pgvector + fuzzy fallback with pg_trgm
PII detection and redaction before database storage
Shipped to MSP (Minimum Sellable Product) stage

devopsSlackBot.problem: 70% of DevOps support requests are routine diagnostics — checking pod status, reading logs, verifying pipelines — that consume engineering time without requiring engineering judgment.
devopsSlackBot.solution: A Slack-based AI agent that autonomously investigates infrastructure issues using kubectl, Azure CLI, Bitbucket, Jira, and Confluence. Read-only by design, with infrastructure knowledge baked into the system prompt so it knows your clusters, naming conventions, and GitOps workflows.
outcomes: 70% of routine requests answerable without human intervention
6 tools with strict read-only guardrails and security validation
79% token reduction via intelligent output compaction
Progressive trust roadmap: read-only → safe actions → approval workflows → full autonomy

medicalDocParser.problem: Medical professionals spend significant time manually extracting diagnoses from documents and coding them to ICD-10 standards. This process is error-prone and delays clinical workflows.
medicalDocParser.solution: An NLP-powered parser that extracts diagnoses from medical documents and automatically maps them to ICD-10 codes. Supports multiple document formats and integrates with clinical systems.
outcomes: >95% OCR accuracy, >90% correct ICD-10 mapping
Multilingual support: Spanish, Catalan, Galician
Processing under 2 min/doc, deployed for Tirea

mcpVitaminD.problem: An assistant asked "can I get vitamin D today?" answers with the generic "15 minutes of sun" line. That answer is wrong most of the time: skin type I in London and skin type V in Madrid need completely different exposure, and above ~40° latitude there are months where synthesis is physically impossible regardless of how long you stay outside.
mcpVitaminD.solution: A remote MCP server that puts the calculation engine behind getvitamind.app directly in the assistant. Six public tools need no account — city search, sun times, daily synthesis window, the full year, live status from real UV and cloud data, and session estimation. Four more read the user's profile, saved cities and sun history over OAuth. A published npm bridge (vitamind-mcp) covers clients that can only launch local commands.
outcomes: 10 tools; the six public ones need no API key or account
Hosted transport plus an npm stdio bridge for local-only clients
Answers computed from NOAA solar geometry, Madronich UV and Holick synthesis models — not a lookup table

vitaminD.problem: Public advice about sun exposure is a single number applied to everyone. It ignores latitude, season, altitude, skin type, age and how much skin is uncovered — the variables that actually decide whether any vitamin D gets made. Below UV index 3, none does, and no amount of time outside changes that.
vitaminD.solution: A PWA that computes the answer instead of looking it up: NOAA solar declination and elevation, Madronich clear-sky UV with van Heuklon ozone and an altitude correction, and Holick synthesis with MED by Fitzpatrick skin type and an age factor. Live UV and cloud cover come from Open-Meteo. Built on Next.js and Supabase with accounts, saved cities, sun history, web push and a daily cron — and shipped in six languages.
outcomes: Live at getvitamind.app, open source under MIT
Six languages (es/en/fr/de/ru/lt), installable PWA with web push
CI quality gate on every push: lint, typecheck, tests and build
